fetched_contents.text: A review of fracture propagation in concrete: fundamentals, experimental techniques, modelling and applications | Magazine of Concrete Research A comprehensive overview of fracture propagation in concrete, covering various aspects ranging from fundamentals to applications and future directions, is presented. The introduction presents an overview of fracture propagation in concrete, emphasising its importance in understanding the behaviour of concrete structures. The fundamentals of fracture propagation are then explored, including concrete as a composite material, crack initiation and propagation mechanisms, types of fractures and the factors that influence fracture propagation. Next, experimental techniques for studying fracture propagation are discussed, encompassing both destructive and non-destructive testing methods, such as acoustic emission, ultrasonic testing, digital image correlation and advanced imaging techniques like X-ray computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy. Modelling approaches, including continuum damage mechanics, the finite-element method, the discrete-element method, the lattice discrete particle model and hybrid models, for simulating and predicting fracture propagation behaviour are then reviewed. The applications of fracture propagation in concrete are highlighted, including structural health monitoring, design optimisation, failure analysis and repair and rehabilitation strategies. Research opportunities for further improvement are addressed. This article should serve as a valuable resource for researchers, engineers and professionals in the field, providing a comprehensive understanding of fracture propagation in concrete and guiding future research endeavours.

fetched_contents.text: Experimental and Analytical Study on Precast High-Strength Concrete Tunnel Lining Segments Reinforced with GFRP Bars | Journal of Composites for Construction Publication: Journal of Composites for Construction Volume 26, Issue 5 Abstract Replacing steel reinforcement with glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) reinforcement is an effective solution to avoid the corrosion problem in precast concrete tunnel-lining (PCTL) segments. In addition, using high-strength concrete (HSC) can improve the durability of concrete in the harsh environment of tunnels. This study pioneers in investigating the structural performance of GFRP-reinforced PCTL segments constructed with HSC by testing four full-scale specimens measuring 3,100 mm in length, 1,500 mm in width, and 250 mm in thickness under a three-point bending load. The investigated parameters included concrete compressive strength [normal-strength concrete (NSC) and HSC], reinforcement ratio (0.48% and 0.90%), and tie configuration (closed ties with U-shaped ties). The results are presented and discussed in terms of cracking behavior, failure mechanism, deflection behavior, strain in reinforcement and concrete, ductility, and deformability. An analytical investigation was carried out to evaluate and modify the existing design provisions (ACI 440.1R-15, CAN/CSA S806-12, CAN/CSA S6-19, and AASHTO 2018) for use in predicting the shear and flexural strength of GFRP-reinforced HSC PCTL segments. The results indicate that using HSC improves the flexural and shear strength of GFRP-reinforced PCTL segments, while it has a minimal effect on the postcracking stiffness and cracking behavior of the specimens. These are typically the pseudo-strain hardening behavior and the ability to develop multiple cracks. The assessment of the tensile load-deformation behavior of these materials is therefore of great importance and is frequently carried out by characterizing the material tensile stress–strain behavior. In this paper an alternative approach to evaluate the tensile performance of SHCC is investigated. The behavior of the material in tension is studied at the level of a single crack. The derived tensile stress-crack opening behavior is utilized to analyze and compare the influence of various composite parameters on the resulting tensile behavior. The deformations occurring during tensile loading are furthermore examined using a digital image-based deformation analysis technique to gain detailed insight into the crack formation, propagation and opening phases. Introduction The recent technological development of a wide variety of fibers has been creating new opportunities for the development of fiber reinforced cementitious composites as structural materials. The behavior of these distinct fibers, which are dispersed in the cementitious matrix, can assume diverse forms and dimensions, allowing the development of numerous functional properties of these materials. In particular, when fiber reinforced cementitious composites are designed to develop strain hardening in tension, so-called Strain Hardening Cementitious Composites (SHCC) are obtained. From the viewpoint of structural design, the strain hardening ability in tension is often referred to as the most relevant feature of SHCC. Pseudo-strain hardening in tension exhibited by SHCC is the consequence of the development of multiple cracks under tensile loading. Tensile hardening at the level of a single crack is the main prerequisite of this composite response to tensile loading. This material property represents a dual advantage in engineering applications: while more cracks develop at the same tensile deformation level, the individual crack openings are significantly smaller. The result of this multiple cracking behavior is enhanced durability and better preservation of functional properties in the structural elements. Conversely, higher energy dissipation ability exists at the level of a single crack, which is amplified by the large number of cracks typically developed. These materials are therefore designed to exhibit high toughness and significant tolerance to damage in tension. Over the past few decades the research carried out in SHCC materials has suggested different approaches to the design of these materials [1], [2]. Engineered Cementitious Composites (ECC), a class of cement-based materials typically reinforced with Polyvinyl Alcohol (PVA) fibers, are an example of SHCC materials showing high tensile strain hardening ability (between 3% and 7% of ultimate tensile strain) at an ultimate tensile strength of 5 MPa [3], [4]. The mechanical behavior in tension of SHCC materials is the result of a delicate balance of multiple factors. The interfacial bonding and fiber pull-out properties, the material parameters of the fibers and of the matrix, the distribution off law sizes in the matrix, the fiber orientation and their dispersion in the matrix play an important role in the resulting composite mechanical behavior. The study of the influence of these parameters individually is complex, given that they perform in a highly coupled manner. The assessment of the tensile performance of SHCC materials is therefore of great importance, for an efficient material design as well as for the appropriate constitutive modeling in structural applications. SHCC materials research has been mostly dedicated to the characterization of their tensile stress–strain behavior, particularly dealing with their unique characteristic, the pseudo-strain hardening ability in tension [4], [5]. The type of test mostly used is the direct tension test using dog bone-shaped (dumbbell-shaped) or coupon specimens [6], [5], [7]. The material tensile stress–strain behavior is thereby assessed as well as the potential of the material to develop multiple cracks. The direct tension tests are experimentally demanding, therefore inverse analysis is also alternatively used to derive indirectly the stress–strain or the stress-separation law from bending tests [8]. Other test setups used are inspired by common test methods adopted to extract the fracture parameters of concrete and other tension softening fiber reinforced cementitious composites. These test methods include the Compact Tension test (CTT), the Wedge Splitting test (WST), the Split Cylinder Tensile Strength Test and the Three Point Bending Test (see for example Refs. [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]). However, the initiation of multiple cracks and the individual particular testing conditions interfere with the explicit and objective characterization of SHCC constitutive properties. In this study an alternative approach to the assessment of the tensile behavior of SHCC materials is investigated. This approach is based on the characterization of the tensile stress-crack opening behavior of SHCC at the level of a single crack. Test-specific factors affecting crack behavior in tie-beam tests

Boundary conditions and loading configuration are central to crack initiation and direction in tie-beam tests. The evidence points to test setups that use reaction forces, loading spans, and effective depths, which are relevant to crack development because they define the stress state and how load is transferred through the specimen [N4-F3]. Tie-beam setups are also described in the context of three-point bending or other load configurations that induce tensile stress in the tension zone, which is where cracking usually begins [N4-R4]. The tie configuration in a related NSC study did not affect cracking behavior, but the test observations emphasize that tie geometry is part of the experimental setup and therefore relevant to crack propagation conditions [N4-F3]. More generally, boundary conditions influence crack direction because concrete crack propagation tends to follow the path of least resistance, and the presence of ties, supports, and geometric constraints can alter this path [N4-F3].

Concrete strength, aggregate content, and specimen geometry also affect crack patterns. The NSC tie-beam study notes that concrete compressive strength was tested in normal-strength concrete specimens, and that tie configuration did not alter cracking behavior [N4-F3]. This suggests that, for these specimens, concrete strength is an important factor, while tie arrangement was less influential. The same evidence also links crack patterns to the test observations, implying that crack development is highly dependent on the material and specimen configuration rather than just the loading scheme alone [N4-F3]. Aggregate-related effects are implied indirectly through the discussion of concrete as a composite material and the influence of aggregate size on mechanical and fracture parameters [N1-F1]. Although the evidence is not explicit about aggregate content in the NSC tie-beam study, it supports a broader conclusion that material heterogeneity—such as aggregate distribution and particle size—can shape micro-crack development and macro-crack formation [N1-F1].

Experimental indicators used to distinguish microcrack from macrocrack behavior include crack patterns, crack spacing, crack width, and deformation observations. In tie-beam tests, crack patterns are explicitly used to select the best test specimen interpretation and to distinguish between different failure modes [N4-R5]. The evidence also mentions crack spacing and crack width as measurable quantities in tension-stiffening tests [N5-R3]. In the broader concrete fracture literature, crack initiation and propagation can be studied through experimental techniques such as acoustic emission, digital image correlation, and scanning electron microscopy, but in the tie-beam context the strongest indicators are crack patterns and deformation behavior [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The distinction between microcrack and macrocrack behavior is also supported by the idea that microcracks grow, coalesce, and eventually form macrocracks, with crack opening and bridging playing a role in the transition [N1-F1][N5-F4]. In tie-beam tests, therefore, the most direct experimental indicators are crack patterns, crack spacing, crack width, and load-displacement response, with crack patterns being especially useful for identifying whether cracks are micro- or macro-scale in origin [N4-R5][N5-R3][N1-F1].

Tie-beam test setup, crack pattern, and failure mode evidence

Test setup features most relevant for tie-beam cracking behavior include the span between reaction forces, effective depth, and the geometry of the loading configuration. The NSC study provides a setup description with a span between reaction forces, effective width, effective depth, and a clear reference to three-point bending or similar loading arrangements [N4-F3]. These dimensions are directly important because they define the stress distribution and the zone where cracking is initiated and propagated. The setup also includes support conditions, which influence how load is transferred and whether the specimen behaves as a simple beam or a more complex composite element [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that tie configuration is part of the test parameters, indicating that reinforcement arrangement and tie spacing can affect crack behavior even if the study does not report a strong effect [N4-F3].

Crack patterns in tie-beam experiments are described as visible, observable features used to interpret test results. The evidence states that photographs of test specimens can assist in selecting the best beam interpretation and that crack patterns are well aligned with experimental observations [N4-R5]. It also notes that crack patterns and concrete crushing are well agreed with the experiment in another study, reinforcing the idea that crack patterns are a primary experimental indicator [N4-R2]. In the NSC tie-beam study, tie configuration did not affect cracking behavior, but the test observations still emphasize crack patterns as a way to interpret the specimen’s response [N4-F3]. Crack patterns are therefore not only descriptive but also diagnostic: they help identify whether cracks are aligned, branching, or localized, and whether they are micro- or macro-scale in origin [N4-R5][N4-R2][N4-F3].

Failure modes associated with cracking in tie-beam tests include cracking behavior itself, concrete crushing, and the transition to failure. The evidence explicitly mentions concrete compression failure and concrete crushing as outcomes of pre-damage loading, with crack patterns and crushing agreeing with experiment [N4-R2]. In the NSC tie-beam study, cracking behavior is clearly a central outcome, and the analytical investigation addresses cracking behavior, failure mechanism, and ductility [N4-F3]. The broader fracture literature indicates that crack propagation leads to loss of stiffness, energy dissipation, and eventual failure [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In tie-beam tests, failure mode is closely tied to load-displacement response: cracking begins as the load increases, stiffness loss becomes apparent during crack propagation, and residual capacity depends on how much damage has accumulated [N3-R1][N4-F3][N5-F4]. Thus, failure is not just a final event but a sequence of crack development, stiffness loss, and eventual collapse, with crack patterns and load-displacement curves serving as complementary indicators [N4-R5][N2-F2][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N7:
Concrete crack initiation and propagation under tensile loading

Tensile stress levels that trigger first crack initiation depend on the material’s tensile strength and the stress state in the specimen. The evidence emphasizes that concrete cracking in tension is often governed by the tensile strength and fracture toughness of the material, with higher tensile strength and fracture toughness associated with better resistance to crack propagation [N2-F2][N2-R4]. In tie-beam tests, cracking is usually initiated in the tension zone, where stress concentrations develop and microcracks begin to form [N4-R5]. The evidence also indicates that crack initiation can be influenced by specimen geometry and boundary conditions, because the test setup defines the stress distribution and crack path [N4-F3][N1-F1]. While the evidence does not provide a precise threshold stress value for NSC, it supports the general principle that cracking begins when the tensile stress exceeds the material’s tensile strength and the stress field is sufficient to cause microcrack growth [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Microcracks evolve into macrocracks through growth, coalescence, and bridging. The micro-to-macro crack mechanisms literature explains that microcracks grow under tensile loading, then coalesce into a macrocrack as the load increases [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that aggregate size and distribution influence micro-crack development and associated macro-crack formation, which means material heterogeneity can accelerate or delay the transition from microcracks to macrocracks [N1-F1]. Bridging is also implied by the discussion of tensile stress-crack opening behavior and strain-hardening responses, where multiple cracks can develop and individual crack openings are reduced, which changes how damage is distributed [N5-F4]. In other words, bridging occurs when fibers, aggregates, or other discontinuities prevent immediate crack propagation, while coalescence occurs when adjacent microcracks merge into a single larger crack [N1-F1][N5-F4]. This transition is not abrupt; it is a progressive process that depends on crack spacing, crack opening, and the presence of reinforcing elements [N5-R3][N5-F4].

Crack propagation depends on tensile stress, specimen size, and material heterogeneity. Higher tensile stress increases the rate of crack propagation, as the evidence shows that peak load and variability can increase with loading rate and pre-notched angle [N2-R1]. Specimen size also matters because larger specimens may experience more heterogeneous stress fields and slower crack propagation due to the longer path of crack growth and the influence of boundary conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1]. Material heterogeneity, particularly aggregate content and particle size, plays a central role in crack behavior. The micro-macro crack mechanisms source states that aggregate size affects mechanical and fracture parameters and micro-crack development, while the NSC tie-beam evidence links crack behavior to concrete compressive strength and tie configuration [N1-F1][N4-F3]. In strain-hardening fiber-reinforced concrete, multiple cracking and strain hardening are achieved by increasing fiber content, showing that material composition can alter crack propagation by promoting distributed cracking rather than single, catastrophic crack growth [N6-R2][N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: tensile stress triggers crack initiation, microcracks evolve into macrocracks through growth and coalescence, and crack propagation is controlled by stress level, specimen size, and the heterogeneity of the material [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2].
node_outputs.N8:
Load-displacement behavior in NSC tie-beam tests

Load-displacement curves in NSC tie-beam tests change with cracking and crack propagation by showing stiffness loss, load redistribution, and residual capacity. The evidence indicates that cracking behavior and failure mechanism are central outcomes of the test, with load-displacement curves reflecting the transition from elastic to post-cracking behavior [N4-F3]. In the NSC tie-beam study, cracking behavior is associated with deflection behavior, ductility, deformability, and postcracking stiffness, while the analytical investigation modifies design provisions to predict flexural capacity [N4-F3]. This means that the load-displacement curve typically rises elastically, then flattens or softens after cracking begins, with a visible loss of stiffness as cracks propagate [N4-F3][N2-F2]. The softening phase begins when the material can no longer carry load efficiently, and this is captured by the loss of stiffness and the eventual reduction in load-carrying capacity [N4-F3][N2-F2]. The evidence also supports the idea that postcracking stiffness and cracking behavior are related, so the load-displacement curve does not simply drop immediately at cracking; instead, it enters a softening phase that depends on fiber content, tie configuration, and material properties [N4-F3][N6-R1].

Residual capacity and failure mode are closely related to crack development. The NSC tie-beam study reports postcracking stiffness and cracking behavior, and the analytical investigation is used to predict flexural capacity and deformation [N4-F3]. This implies that residual capacity is not zero after cracking; it is instead reduced but still present, and the magnitude depends on how much damage has accumulated [N4-F3]. Failure mode is associated with cracking because the study explicitly discusses cracking behavior, failure mechanism, and ductility [N4-F3]. In the broader fracture literature, crack propagation leads to energy dissipation, loss of stiffness, and eventual failure, with the failure mode reflecting the dominant cracking pattern and the degree of damage accumulation [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In tie-beam tests, failure is therefore not just a single point but a sequence: cracking initiates, crack propagation reduces stiffness, residual capacity decreases, and the final failure mode depends on whether the cracks localize, spread, or coalesce [N4-F3][N2-F2][N1-F1]. Overall, the load-displacement behavior in NSC tie-beam tests is characterized by an initial elastic response, a softening phase after cracking, and a failure mode that is determined by the extent and distribution of cracking [N4-F3][N2-F2][N5-F4].

## Integrated explanation of how tensile load influences crack initiation, propagation, and load-displacement behavior in NSC tie-beam tests

### 1) How tensile load influences crack initiation

Tensile loading in concrete generally initiates cracking when the tensile stress exceeds the material’s tensile strength and the stress field is sufficient to cause microcrack growth [N2-F2][N4-R5]. In NSC tie-beam tests, cracking is typically initiated in the tension zone, where the test setup defines the stress distribution and where microcracks first appear [N4-F3][N4-R5]. The evidence also suggests that crack initiation is not just a function of tensile stress alone: boundary conditions, loading configuration, and specimen geometry all shape the stress state and the path along which cracking begins [N4-F3][N2-F2]. In other words, the same tensile stress may produce different crack initiation responses depending on how the load is applied and how the specimen is supported.

Crack initiation is therefore tied to the local stress state and the material’s tensile strength. The broader fracture literature indicates that higher tensile strength and fracture toughness improve resistance to crack propagation [N2-F2][N2-R4]. In NSC tie-beam tests, concrete compressive strength is a key test parameter, and the evidence suggests that tie configuration may not strongly affect cracking behavior, but the test setup and geometry still determine where and how cracks form [N4-F3]. This means that crack initiation in tie-beam tests is a combination of material behavior and loading conditions, with the first crack usually appearing in the tension zone under increasing tensile load [N4-R5][N4-F3].

### 2) How tensile load influences micro- and macro-crack propagation

Under continued tensile loading, microcracks evolve into macrocracks through growth, coalescence, and bridging [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The micro-to-macro crack mechanisms literature explains that microcracks grow under tensile loading, and as load increases, they coalesce until a macrocrack forms [N1-F1]. The same source notes that aggregate size and distribution influence micro-crack development and associated macro-crack formation, meaning material heterogeneity can accelerate or delay the transition from microcracks to macrocracks [N1-F1]. Bridging is also implied by the discussion of tensile stress-crack opening behavior and strain-hardening responses, where multiple cracks can develop and individual crack openings are reduced, changing how damage is distributed [N5-F4].

Crack propagation is further controlled by specimen size and material heterogeneity. The evidence shows that higher tensile stress increases crack propagation, and that peak load and variability can increase with loading rate and pre-notched angle [N2-R1]. Specimen size also matters because larger specimens may experience more heterogeneous stress fields and slower crack propagation due to the longer path of crack growth and boundary conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In strain-hardening fiber-reinforced concrete, multiple cracking and strain hardening are achieved by increasing fiber content, showing that material composition can alter crack propagation by promoting distributed cracking rather than single, catastrophic crack growth [N6-R2][N6-R1]. So, in NSC tie-beam tests, microcrack propagation leads to macrocrack formation through progressive coalescence and bridging, while the overall crack propagation rate depends on tensile stress, specimen size, and material heterogeneity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2].
